common_name: Scarlet Heaven Itoh Peony (Deep Red Single-to-Semi-Double Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Set container-grown plants in early to mid fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with the crown no more than an inch below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Scarlet Heaven carries large, loosely cupped flowers in a saturated true red, opening nearly single to lightly semi-double with a prominent cluster of golden stamens at the center. Like other Itoh hybrids it combines the heavy, well-branched stems and finely cut, glossy foliage of a tree peony parent with the herbaceous habit of a lactiflora parent, so the whole plant dies back cleanly to the ground each fall rather than persisting as a woody shrub. Give it a permanent spot in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and avoid disturbing the crown once established, since the clump will take a couple of seasons to settle in before reaching full flower production.

common_name: Hidden Treasure Itoh Peony (Soft Yellow Double Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container divisions in early fall so roots can establish before frost, setting the crown just below grade in rich, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Hidden Treasure produces fully double, buttery soft yellow flowers held well above dark green, deeply dissected foliage reminiscent of its tree peony parentage. The strong, self-supporting stems rarely need staking even under the weight of the large blooms, and the foliage stays attractive and disease-resistant through the summer after flowering ends. As with other intersectional hybrids, give it a permanent, undisturbed site in fertile, well-drained soil, since clumps can take a season or two to build up to a full flush of bloom.

common_name: Pink Double Dandy Itoh Peony (Rose-Pink Fully Double Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Set divisions in fall 4-6 weeks ahead of hard frost in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping the crown shallow so new eyes can push through easily each spring.

directions: Pink Double Dandy opens rounded, fully double flowers in clear rose-pink, fading gently toward the petal edges as the bloom ages, and carries a light fragrance typical of many Itoh selections. Its sturdy, well-branched stems and mounded habit keep the heavy flowers upright without support, and the clean, dark green foliage resists the leaf spot that can trouble older lactiflora cultivars late in the season. Plant in a permanent location with excellent drainage, since like other peonies it dislikes wet feet and resents being moved once settled.

common_name: All That Jazz Itoh Peony (Coral-Rose Semi-Double Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, allowing roots to establish before the ground freezes.

directions: All That Jazz bears large, semi-double flowers that open a warm coral-rose and soften with age, the loose ring of petals revealing a bright gold center of stamens. The vigorous, bushy plant builds into a full mound of deeply cut foliage that stays tidy through the growing season and needs no staking even in exposed sites. Give it full sun for the best flower color and stem strength, with a little afternoon shade appreciated in hotter climates, and leave the clump undisturbed once planted.

common_name: Keiko Itoh Peony (Peach-Pink Double Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root divisions in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, setting the crown shallow and leaving ample room for the clump to spread over time.

directions: Keiko produces densely packed double flowers in a soft peach-pink that deepens slightly toward the base of the petals, giving each bloom a gentle two-tone glow. Flowers are carried on thick, rigid stems above a mounded clump of glossy, dissected foliage that holds its color and form well past the bloom period. As with other Itoh hybrids, the top growth dies back completely in fall, so mark the planting location and avoid disturbing the dormant crown through winter.

common_name: Flame Peony (Early Single Red-Orange Hybrid Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with eyes set 1-2 in deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the clump room since early hybrid peonies often grow wider than standard lactiflora cultivars.

directions: Flame bears single, saucer-shaped flowers in a vivid orange-red that lives up to the cultivar's name, each bloom centered on a bright boss of golden stamens that attracts pollinators heavily. It opens among the earliest of the herbaceous peonies, extending the start of the peony season ahead of most lactiflora doubles, and its sturdy stems rarely require staking. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and leave the clump undisturbed for years, since mature plants flower far more heavily than recently divided ones.

common_name: Nippon Beauty Peony (Dark Red Japanese-Form Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Nippon Beauty is one of the older Japanese-form lactiflora cultivars grown in American gardens, with a single to semi-double ring of deep red guard petals surrounding a dense tuft of narrow, modified staminodes in a contrasting golden hue. This 'Japanese' or 'anemone' form gives the flower a lighter, more open look than a full double, and the sturdy stems hold it upright without staking. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and divide only when clumps become congested, since peonies otherwise thrive for decades undisturbed.

common_name: Sword Dance Peony (Early Single Red Hybrid Peony)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, setting eyes shallow so new growth emerges easily the following spring.

directions: Sword Dance carries single, brilliant red flowers with crepe-textured petals surrounding a bright center of yellow stamens, opening early in the peony season on upright, well-branched stems. Its single form keeps the flowers lighter than double cultivars, so they stand up well to spring wind and rain without flopping or needing support. Site it in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and expect bloom to improve noticeably as the clump matures over several seasons.

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with eyes set 1-2 in deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this older French cultivar rewards patience, taking a few seasons to reach full bloom.

directions: Avalanche is a nineteenth-century French lactiflora cultivar with large, creamy white flowers that open loosely double, the outer guard petals occasionally flushed with the faintest blush of pink near the base. Its flowers carry a light, sweet fragrance that makes it a favorite for cutting, and the plant forms a dense, upright clump of glossy dark green foliage that stays attractive well after bloom. Grow in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and avoid dividing more often than necessary, since this heirloom cultivar can take time to settle back into heavy flowering after disturbance.

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in early fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, setting eyes no more than 1-2 in below the surface so they are not slow to emerge in spring.

directions: Tourangelle is a French heirloom lactiflora prized for its full double blooms in a soft, shifting blend of salmon-pink and cream, a color combination often compared to hydrangea flowers, which fades gracefully as each bloom ages. The large flowers are heavy enough to benefit from peony hoops or light staking in open, windy gardens, and the tall, vigorous clump makes a good back-of-border choice among other old-fashioned perennials. Plant in full sun in deep, fertile soil, and give it room to mature undisturbed, since antique lactiflora cultivars often improve in bloom quality for many years after planting.

common_name: Philomele Peony (Pink and Cream Japanese-Form Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping eyes shallow; this antique French cultivar is slow to re-establish after division, so disturb it as little as possible.

directions: Philomele is a nineteenth-century Japanese-form lactiflora with a ring of rose-pink guard petals surrounding a contrasting center of narrow, creamy-yellow petaloids, a bicolor combination that sets it apart from the solid-color doubles common in modern catalogs. The lighter, more open bloom structure of the Japanese form lets the flower hold up well in rain compared with heavier bomb-form cultivars. Grow in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and expect this heirloom to reward an undisturbed, well-established clump with its best display.

common_name: Mother's Choice Peony (White Bomb-Form Exhibition Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall with eyes set 1-2 in deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake the strong stems ahead of bloom since the large flowers can be heavy.

directions: Mother's Choice bears large, rounded bomb-form flowers in pure white, with a faint blush sometimes visible at the petal bases when the bloom first opens, held on tall, sturdy stems above glossy dark green foliage. The classic exhibition form, with a tight dome of petaloids rising from a ring of broad outer guard petals, has made it a long-standing favorite among peony show exhibitors and collectors of white-flowered cultivars. Plant in full sun in deep, fertile soil, and give the clump several seasons to mature, since bomb-form lactiflora cultivars often take time to build up to their fullest bloom.

common_name: Burma Ruby Peony (Single Ruby-Red Hybrid Peony)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, setting eyes shallow and leaving the clump undisturbed once it is in the ground.

directions: Burma Ruby produces single, satin-textured flowers in a deep ruby red, the broad petals cupping loosely around a bright cluster of golden stamens that stands out sharply against the dark color. As a hybrid peony it tends to bloom earlier than most lactiflora doubles and carries noticeably strong, upright stems that rarely need staking even in open sites. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, and expect flowering to improve each year as the clump builds size.

common_name: Charlie's White Peony (Late Single White Japanese-Form Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, setting eyes 1-2 in deep to give the clump a full season to establish before winter.

directions: Charlie's White opens pure white, single to semi-double flowers late in the peony season, each bloom centered on a dense boss of bright yellow stamens that gives strong contrast against the petals. Its late bloom time helps extend the garden display after most early and midseason lactiflora cultivars have finished, and the open, single form sheds rain well without weighing down the stems. Plant in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil, and leave the clump undisturbed for the richest bloom in later years.
